title: Second FRRR round targets Alfred and Queensland flood communities as insurers' grants stay small
full_text:
Community groups in Queensland’s disaster-hit regions have a second chance at recovery funding this storm season, after an earlier round drew fewer applications than expected from the hardest-hit areas.
The Foundation for Rural & Regional Renewal’s (FRRR) Rebuilding Futures program has opened a $250,000 round, funded by Suncorp, for communities affected by Tropical Cyclone Alfred and the Western Queensland Trough and Flooding. Not-for-profit and grassroots organisations in local government areas with a disaster declaration for either event can apply for up to $25,000. The money can go towards mental health and wellbeing, social connection, emergency planning, preparedness equipment and small-scale infrastructure. Applications close at 5pm AEDT on November 26, and funding will be awarded in February 2027.
The round follows one IB Australia reported on in July, where a separate stream was included for the same two events, and FRRR flagged fewer applications than expected from Alfred and western Queensland communities.
FRRR head of granting Jill Karena said recovery in the west had been slower, more complex and more resource-intensive. “While Cyclone Alfred caused concentrated damage through wind, coastal erosion and flash flooding in southeast Queensland, the western Queensland floods presented a different challenge. Much of the region was underwater for a long time, leading to community isolation, agricultural losses and extensive infrastructure damage across a vast area,” she said.
Suncorp chief executive consumer insurance Michael Miller said community organisations “are often at the heart of a community’s recovery, helping people rebuild connections and a sense of normality after a disaster”.
Suncorp is one of several insurers funding community resilience. Earlier this month, the QBE Foundation awarded $600,000 to 12 community organisations, $50,000 each, with four of the grants going to climate resilience work, including in flood-exposed Lismore. In March, RACQ launched a Resilient Energy Centre program funding up to $500,000 in solar, batteries and satellite backup, so community clubs can keep power and communications running during disasters. IAG’s NRMA Insurance runs a Help Fund backing climate-resilience initiatives.
Set against the losses, these programs are small. Suncorp’s July guidance put its FY26 hazard costs at about $2.02 billion, roughly $250 million above its allowance, across 18 events.
For brokers with not-for-profit, sporting club or community group clients in Alfred or western Queensland flood areas, the deadline is worth passing on. FRRR is running a grantseeker webinar on November 2 at 1pm AEST. Grants on this scale can help a community recover, but they will not shift a region’s risk profile enough to move premiums.
author: Camille Joyce Lisay
